title: A connection pool on a counting semaphore

blocks.text: The page's `ConnectionPool` guards N connections with a `Semaphore(N)`: `acquire()` takes a permit (waiting while there are none) and then a connection; `release` puts the connection back and returns the permit. The page also warns about **permit inflation**: a semaphore enforces no upper bound, so one release too many silently lets one more thread in. Guard against it in your own code.
Write `Pool<R>`, built from a list of resources:

items: `R acquire()` waits until a resource is free and returns it.
`R tryAcquire(long timeout, TimeUnit unit)` waits **at most** `timeout`; `null` if nothing came free.

`void release(R resource)` returns a leased resource. A resource that is not **currently leased** (released twice, or never handed out by this pool) is refused with `IllegalArgumentException` and changes nothing. Leases are tracked by **object identity**: a different object that merely `equals` a leased one was not leased.
`int available()` is the number of free resources.

blocks.text: The tests cannot make a woken `acquire()` run between two steps of `release`, or make two threads release the same resource at the same instant, so those orderings are not graded. Get them right anyway: put the resource back before returning the permit, and check and remove a lease in one step.

rows: that `acquire()` waits, then returns that same `db-1` object

cases.says: Resources are leased and returned, and available() counts the free ones.
acquire() on an empty pool waits, and gets the very resource that is released.
A timed acquire on an empty pool gives up after its timeout and returns null.
A timed acquire on an empty pool waits, and gets a resource released before its timeout.
Releasing the same resource twice is refused and does not inflate the permit count.
A resource that is equal to a leased one but is not that object is refused.
A timeout of 250,000 microseconds or 1,600 ms waits that long in full: the unit is honoured and nothing is rounded to whole seconds.

concepts: A Semaphore(N) lets at most N holders at once: acquire() takes a permit and waits while none is free, release() returns one.
A semaphore enforces no upper bound, so releasing more than was acquired inflates the count; application code must guard it.
tryAcquire(timeout, unit) waits at most the timeout for a permit and returns false when none came.
